chapters.title: Chapter 1: Why Financial Statements Matter to Managers

lessons.title: The Annual Report Tour: Where to Find the Numbers in an Indian Company's Filings

children.text: Your managing director forwards a PDF at 9pm with one line: "Their margins look better than ours. Find out why, by Friday." The file is a competitor's annual report. It is 312 pages long. The first 90 pages are photographs of smiling employees, a chairman's letter and an infographic about purpose. Somewhere inside is the number you need.

An annual report is not written to be read front to back. It is a filing cabinet with a fixed set of drawers, in a fixed order, at every Indian company. Once you know the drawers, you can find any number in about ten minutes. That is the whole skill this lesson teaches.

body.text: The numbers you need are almost never in the glossy opening pages. They are in the financial statements and, more often, in the notes that follow them.

children.text: The Drawers: How an Indian Annual Report Is Organised

Every annual report of a listed Indian company carries the same core sections, in roughly this order. Only the first few are written to persuade you. The rest are written because the law requires them, which is exactly why they are more useful.

body.caption: The standard sections of an Indian annual report

cells: Chairman and CEO letters, awards, photographs, selected ratios chosen by the company
You want the management story, with a pinch of salt
Management explains the year: industry trends, segment performance, risks, outlook
You need the why behind a number you already found
Dividend, reserves, related party deals, CSR spending, employee remuneration details
You need governance or CSR facts
Board composition, committees, and ESG disclosures in SEBI's standard BRSR format
You need ESG, diversity or board data
The auditor's opinion, key audit matters, and the CARO annexure
Always, before you trust any number
Balance sheet, statement of profit and loss, cash flow statement, statement of changes in equity
Accounting policies plus the breakup of nearly every line above
You need detail, which is most of the time
Meeting agenda, resolutions, director appointments, remuneration approvals
You are tracking a specific resolution

body.text: The notes are usually the longest part of the report and the part managers skip. If a P&L line says "Other expenses ₹4,120 crore", the note behind it splits that into rent, power, travel, marketing, legal fees and more. Benchmarking questions are almost always answered in the notes, not on the face of the statements.

children.text: The layout of the statements themselves is not the company's choice.
Schedule III
of the Companies Act, 2013 prescribes the format, which is why an Asian Paints balance sheet and an Eternal balance sheet carry their lines in the same order.

markDefs.definition: The schedule to the Companies Act, 2013 that prescribes the format and line-item order of the balance sheet and statement of profit and loss. It is why financial statements of two unrelated Indian companies look near identical.

children.text: Standalone or Consolidated: Read the Right One

Most reports contain two complete sets of financial statements, and managers routinely quote the wrong one. Standalone covers only the parent company. Consolidated adds every subsidiary it controls, line by line, after removing transactions between group companies.

columns.label: Standalone
points: Only the parent company's own operations
Excludes subsidiaries in India and abroad
Used for dividends, taxes and statutory filings
Useful when you want to isolate the core entity

columns.label: Consolidated
points: Parent plus all subsidiaries as one economic unit
Internal group sales are removed so nothing is double counted
The set investors, analysts and lenders actually track
Use this for company-level comparisons unless told otherwise

children.text: The gap can be large. For the year ended 31 March 2025, Infosys reported these two sets of numbers.

body.title: Infosys FY25: standalone vs consolidated (₹ crore)
How much do the subsidiaries add?
body.prompt: Infosys reported FY25 revenue of ₹1,62,990 crore on a consolidated basis and ₹1,36,592 crore on a standalone basis. How much revenue comes from outside the parent company, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: ₹1,62,990 crore minus ₹1,36,592 crore = ₹26,398 crore, about 16% of consolidated revenue. Quote the standalone figure in a competitor comparison and you understate Infosys by more than ₹26,000 crore.

body.title: Which set includes the group?
body.textWithBlank: Financial statements that combine the parent company with all its subsidiaries are called ___ financial statements.
body.explanation: Consolidated statements treat the group as one economic unit and eliminate transactions between group companies. Standalone statements cover the parent alone.

children.text: Where to Get the Documents
You never need to email a competitor's investor relations team. Everything below is public and free.
Company website:
the investor relations section carries annual reports, quarterly results and investor presentations, usually going back ten years or more.
NSE and BSE:
every filing a listed company makes reaches the exchanges first, often before it appears on the company website.
MCA portal:
unlisted and private companies do not publish annual reports publicly, but their filed financial statements can be bought as documents on the MCA portal for a small fee.
screener.in:
ten years of P&L, balance sheet and cash flow data already pulled into tables, plus links to the underlying filings. The fastest first stop for a comparison.

body.label: NSE India: corporate filings and annual reports
body.description: Search by company name or symbol to download annual reports as filed with the exchange.

body.label: MCA: View Company or LLP Master Data
body.description: For unlisted and private companies: check registration and capital details first, then buy filed financial statements through View Public Documents.

body.text: Investor presentations and press releases are easier to read than annual reports, and that is exactly the risk. They carry company-chosen measures such as adjusted EBITDA or constant currency growth, which no accounting standard defines. Use them for context, then verify every number you plan to quote against the audited statements.

children.text: The Reporting Calendar

Knowing when numbers arrive matters as much as knowing where they sit. Under Regulation 33 of SEBI's Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements Regulations, 2015, a listed company must file quarterly results within 45 days of the quarter end, and audited annual results within 60 days of the financial year end. The full annual report follows later, ahead of the AGM.

body.title: A listed company's reporting year, FY26

events.title: Financial year begins
events.description: FY26 starts. Budgets and targets for the year are locked.

events.title: Q1 results
events.description: Unaudited results for April to June, subject to a limited review by the auditor, due within 45 days of 30 June.

events.title: Q2 and half-year results
events.description: The half-year mark, where most companies revisit their full-year guidance.

events.title: Q3 results
events.description: October to December. For consumer companies this is the festive quarter.

events.title: Q4 and audited annual results
events.description: Due within 60 days of 31 March. The first time you see full-year audited numbers.

events.title: Annual report and AGM
events.description: The complete annual report, with notes, auditor's report and MD&A, is published ahead of the annual general meeting.

body.label: Audited vs reviewed
body.value: Only the annual numbers are audited
body.context: Quarterly results are unaudited and carry a limited review report, which is a lighter check than a full audit. If your analysis has to hold up in a board meeting, use the annual audited statements.

children.text: Finding Any Number in Ten Minutes
This is the routine. It works on any Indian annual report, whatever the company.
Open the PDF and go straight to the index or the bookmarks pane. Jump to "Consolidated Financial Statements".
Go to the statement of profit and loss for P&L lines, or the balance sheet for balances. Read the current year column and the previous year column beside it.
Note the small note number printed next to the line you care about, for example "Other expenses 27".
Jump to that note. This is where the breakup lives: rent, power and fuel, travel, advertising, professional fees.
Cross check the story in the MD&A, which usually explains any line that moved sharply.
Read the auditor's report, especially the opinion paragraph and the key audit matters, before you circulate anything.

body.title: Where does the breakup live?
body.question: A competitor's consolidated statement of profit and loss shows "Employee benefit expenses ₹9,840 crore". You need to know how much of that is gratuity and provident fund. Where do you look?
options: The note to accounts referenced against that line
body.explanation: Every line on the face of the statements carries a note reference. The note for employee benefit expenses splits it into salaries and wages, contribution to provident and other funds, gratuity, share-based payments and staff welfare.

body.title: What the auditor's opinion actually means

children.text: The auditor's report opens with an opinion paragraph. There are four possible outcomes, and the difference matters.
Unmodified, or clean, opinion:
the statements give a true and fair view. This is the normal case.
Qualified opinion:
everything is fine except for specific issues, which the auditor lists. Read those paragraphs closely.
Adverse opinion:
the statements do not give a true and fair view. Rare and serious.
Disclaimer of opinion:
the auditor could not gather enough evidence to form any opinion at all. Treat the numbers with real caution.

Below the opinion sit the key audit matters, the areas the auditor found most difficult or most dependent on judgement, such as revenue recognition on long-term contracts or the valuation of goodwill. They are a free list of the riskiest numbers in the report.

body.title: Friday deadline: the margin question
body.scenario: Your MD wants to know why a listed competitor in your industry reports a better operating margin than your company. You have their latest annual report and yours, and two days.
body.prompt: Which sections do you open, in what order, and what will you actually compare?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Use consolidated statements for both companies, and confirm both cover the same 12 months ending 31 March.
2. From each statement of profit and loss, pull revenue from operations and every major expense line, then convert each line into a percentage of revenue. Margin gaps come from cost lines, so that is where you have to look.
3. Open the notes for the two or three lines with the biggest percentage gap, most often cost of materials, employee benefit expenses and other expenses, and compare the components.
4. Read the segment note. A competitor can look more profitable simply because of a different business mix, such as a larger services segment.
5. Read the MD&A for management's own explanation of margin movement: price increases, cost programmes, one-off items.
6. Check the auditor's report and any exceptional items. A one-time gain can flatter a single year.
7. Present the gap as a bridge, for example "3.2 percentage points, of which 2.1 is raw material cost and 0.8 is employee cost", rather than as a single verdict.

body.title: Your first annual report tour
steps: Download the latest annual report of your employer or a competitor listed on NSE or BSE.
Find the page where the consolidated financial statements begin, and note the page number.
Write down revenue, net profit and cash from operations for the current and previous year.
Pick the largest expense line and open its note to see the breakup.
Read the auditor's opinion paragraph and check whether it is unmodified.
Find one sentence in the MD&A that explains a number you found, and save it for your next review meeting.

cards.definition: Financial statements of the parent company alone, excluding its subsidiaries.
Parent plus all subsidiaries combined as one unit, with intra-group transactions removed.
The detailed breakup and accounting policies behind every line of the statements.
Management Discussion and Analysis: management's unaudited narrative on the year's performance, risks and outlook.
The areas the auditor judged most significant or most difficult, listed in the auditor's report.
The lighter check applied to quarterly results. Only annual results are fully audited.
Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report, the ESG disclosure format required of the top 1,000 listed companies by market capitalisation.

points: Annual reports follow a fixed order. The persuasive sections come first and the audited numbers come later.
Notes to accounts hold the breakup of nearly every line and answer most benchmarking questions.
Read consolidated statements for a group view, and standalone only when you specifically want the parent company.
Annual reports are free on company websites, NSE and BSE, with screener.in as the fastest first stop and the MCA portal for unlisted companies.
Quarterly results are unaudited and due within 45 days of quarter end. Annual audited results are due within 60 days of year end.
Check the auditor's opinion and the key audit matters before you circulate any number.

body.text: Infosys figures are FY25 consolidated and standalone numbers as reported on screener.in, used only to illustrate the difference between the two sets. Nothing here is investment advice, and filing timelines can change when SEBI amends its regulations.
